personas.role: Fixed pole. Always argues from rights, always for the full market policy.
Swing, market side. Practical card is silent on the standard; common-good card names it.
Swing, control side. Practical card: experts should manage it. Moral card: borrows rights vocabulary for a collective conclusion.
Fixed pole. Always argues morally, always for control. Also the opposition slot every crisis.

crises.title: Drought
crises.trigger: There's a drought across the whole valley. Every farm pumps from the same underground water, and there isn't enough to go around. Your crops that need lots of water will grow only half as much this season.

policies.name: Water rights you can buy and sell
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Every farm pumps for itself, no price limits
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Public water company
policies.immediate: You get water at cost this season.
policies.drag: You pay a water bill from now on.

policies.name: Water board with a rising pumping tax
policies.immediate: The water board taxes every gallon you pump, and the more you pump, the higher the rate. You can afford to water about 60% of your thirsty crops. The rest dry up and die.
policies.drag: The pumping tax stays, so watering more than that never pays.
policies.modifier: waterTax: rises per unit pumped; effective irrigationCap ≈ 0.6 × planted

policies.name: Water handed out by need
policies.immediate: Big farms get less water than small ones. Whatever you can't water dies.
policies.drag: The limit stays, and you're not allowed to buy or sell water.

crises.title: Blight
crises.trigger: A crop disease is spreading through the valley. It came in on bad seed, and every farm that plants that seed spreads it to the fields next door. It has already killed one of your crops, which will take two seasons to grow back.

policies.name: Buy seed from anyone, at your own risk
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Optional 'checked safe' label from seed sellers
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Optional county seed check, for a fee
policies.immediate: You can get your seed checked, so it's safe to replant sooner. Your crop grows back in one season instead of two.
policies.drag: You pay a fee every time you plant.

policies.name: Required seed checks and planting permits
policies.immediate: Every farm's seed is checked, so nothing can reinfect your fields. You can replant right away.
policies.drag: You have to wait for a permit every time you plant.

policies.name: A valley seed board controls all seed and picks your crops
policies.immediate: You get new seed for free.
policies.drag: The state decides what you grow from now on.

crises.title: Price crash
crises.trigger: Times are hard across the country, and people are spending less on everything, food included. The companies that buy the valley's crops have cut what they pay. For the next two seasons, everything you sell brings in 40% less. Some farms in the valley won't survive it.

policies.name: Leave prices alone
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Let farmers lock in next year's price now
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Short-term loans
policies.immediate: You get a loan now.
policies.drag: You pay it back over the next four seasons.

policies.name: Lowest-price guarantee, paid for by a harvest tax
policies.immediate: Prices drop only 10% instead of 40%. A valley relief fund covers the difference.
policies.drag: From now on, 10% of every harvest's income goes into the relief fund.

policies.name: The state buys all crops at set prices
policies.immediate: Prices stay where they were before the crash.
policies.drag: You have to sell to the state, only as much as they allow, at a price that never goes up.

crises.title: Eminent domain
crises.trigger: The county is damming the river to build a reservoir, so the towns downstream have water all year. The plan runs right through your east fields.

policies.name: No taking land. The county builds on its own land.
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Only buy from people who want to sell
policies.immediate: The county offers to buy 4 tiles at the edge of your farm for 20% more than they're worth. You can say no.

policies.name: Take the land, pay full price
policies.immediate: The county takes 4 tiles at the edge of your farm and pays full price. You can't say no.

policies.name: Take the land, pay a "fair" price
policies.immediate: The county takes a wider strip: 6 tiles, some with crops still on them, and pays you half what they're worth.

policies.name: Take the best land for the common good, pay nothing
policies.immediate: The county takes whatever route it likes best: your 8 best tiles, and pays nothing.

crises.note: Survey stakes appear; no farm effect until a policy passes.

crises.title: Overproduction
crises.trigger: Your farm has had its best year ever. Other farmers complain to the council that you grow so much, they can't sell their own crops. There's so much on the market that the price of your top crop has already dropped 25%. They want the council to step in.

policies.name: Leave it alone
policies.immediate: None

policies.name: Farmers' group you can choose to join
policies.immediate: A farmers' group offers you a deal. If every member grows less of the top crop, prices go back up, and you'd get 15% more for yours. Your side: grow it on 5 tiles or fewer. You can say no.
policies.drag: Your top crop is limited to 5 tiles. That's your side of the deal.

policies.name: Fee on extra crops
policies.immediate: You pay a fee for every tile of your top crop past 5, and you have to wait to sell the extra.

policies.name: Limits on how much you can plant
policies.immediate: Your top crop gets plowed under past 5 tiles.
policies.drag: You can't grow more than 5 tiles of your top crop.

policies.name: Ban the crop and even things out
policies.immediate: Your top crop is banned, and every tile of it is destroyed.
policies.drag: Anything you grow above the valley average gets taken at every harvest.

crises.note: In the real game, trigger off farm value above a threshold.

cards.argument: Water sitting underground is worth nothing to anyone. It's just wet rock until somebody drills a well and pumps it up. Whoever does that work turned it into something useful, and that's what makes it theirs. Needing water doesn't give your neighbor a claim on it, and the council never drilled a thing. If someone wants your water, they can offer you a deal.

No water board can keep track of what every farm needs. A price can. When water costs more, every farmer switches to crops that need less and stops wasting a drop. It happens on its own, and it happens fast. So let every farm pump for itself and sell water at whatever price it can get. No board, no price limits.

If you care about the families who'd be hurt worst, a free market is still the answer. A board hands water to whoever has friends on the board. In a free market any farm, big or small, can buy the water it needs and sell what it doesn't. That's what's best for everyone, and for the poorest most of all.
Every well pulls from the same underground water. When one farm pumps more, the farm next door gets less. The scientists have the numbers. Let the water board decide how much each farm can take.

It's unfair that some people should suffer because they aren't wealthy. Prices are fine, but a price alone sends water to whoever has the most money. So let the water board put a tax on pumping that climbs the more you pump. Small farms barely feel it. The big pumpers pay for the water they're taking from everyone else.

The water under this valley belongs to all of us, not to whoever drills the deepest well. Prices have no place in a drought. A valley water board should work out what each farm needs and hand that out, with no buying or selling. Nobody goes without, and nobody gets extra.

You picked the seed, so the risk is yours. If your seed ruins your neighbor's field, you owe them for it, and that's between you and them. But nobody gets to decide ahead of time what you're allowed to plant. A seller who sells bad seed loses customers. That's all the checking a farm needs.

Nobody can check seed faster than the people buying it. Let seed sellers earn a 'checked safe' label, and farmers will pay extra for labeled seed. Sellers of bad seed lose their customers, bad seed stops getting planted, and the disease has nowhere to start. Required permits just hold up every planting for weeks.

Think about the small farms. One more lost harvest and they're gone. A county permit office takes weeks, and the big farms always seem to get their permits first. A 'checked safe' label works for everyone: a small farm can see which seed is safe and plant it the same day. That's what's best for everyone, and for the small farms most of all.

Crop disease doesn't stop at the fence. One careless farmer can infect the whole valley. The plant experts know which seed is clean. Required checks just put what they know to use before it's too late.

Everyone has a right to a harvest that a neighbor's bad seed can't take away. Buy seed from whoever you like, but the county checks every batch before it goes in the ground, and a permit shows yours passed. One careless farm shouldn't be able to ruin the families around it.

The valley's harvest belongs to everyone who needs it to eat, so no farm should get to gamble with it. A valley seed board should be the only source of seed. It hands out clean seed to every farm for free and decides who plants what, so one disease can never sweep through the whole valley again.

A price is whatever someone is willing to pay. Nobody owes you last year's price. Making buyers or taxpayers cover the difference is taking their money by law. You can sell, wait, or switch crops. That's your call.

Low prices fix themselves. Some farms switch crops, there's less to sell, and prices climb back up. Let farmers lock in a price for next year's crop before it falls any further, and they can get through this without a cent of tax money.

Propping up prices helps the biggest farms most and makes food cost more for the families in the valley with the least. If you care about them, let prices fall. Cheap food is the best thing that can happen to a poor family, even if some farms close over it.
Crop prices swing too high and too low. Economists have known this for a hundred years. A guaranteed lowest price evens out the swings, so good farms don't go under after one bad year.

Everyone who grows our food has a right to make a living from it. A family shouldn't lose its farm over a bad year it didn't cause. So take a small share of every harvest into a valley relief fund, and use it to guarantee a lowest price. Above that floor, the market can do what it likes.

Food shouldn't be a gamble, and a farmer's living shouldn't depend on luck. A valley buying board should buy every crop at one fair price and sell it on. Every farm gets the same deal: no windfalls, no ruin. We all eat, so we all share the risk.
The county can want a reservoir all it likes. Wanting something doesn't give you a right to it. If the project needs your land, it needs your signature, and the price is whatever you'll agree to.
Forcing people to sell looks cheap on paper. In real life you get lawsuits, delays, and land bought at a price nobody checked. Buy from people who want to sell, and the reservoir gets built faster.

When the county can force a sale, it's never the big farms that get bulldozed. It's the small ones that can't afford a lawyer. If you care about them, make the county buy only from willing sellers, at a price the seller agrees to. That's what's best for everyone.

You can't route a reservoir around everyone who says no. The engineers have done the survey. One owner shouldn't add three miles and two years to a project for the whole county. Take the strip, pay the set price, and move on.
Thousands of families downstream have a right to water all year. One farm's east fields can't come before that. Take the land, but pay the owner fairly. Then everyone gets what they need.

Nobody made this land. It was here before any of us, and the river that runs through it belongs to every family downstream. So the county should take the land the reservoir needs, even the best land, and pay nothing for what was never really anyone's.

Nobody is owed customers. The other farmers lost sales because buyers chose your crops, and buyers have every right to choose. A council that punishes you for growing more is punishing the whole point of farming.

Planting limits don't fix having too much of a crop. They just lock the problem in place. Prices drop, slower farms switch crops, and in two seasons it sorts itself out. If farmers want to control supply, they can join a group by choice, and nobody has to plow crops under.

Think of the families in the valley with the least. Cheap food is the best thing that can happen to them, and planting limits take it away to protect farms that were already comfortable. If growers want to team up, let them. But don't make the poorest families pay for it.

Farm markets don't fix themselves. They swing too far and take whole farms down with them. The county farm office knows how much can safely be planted. Planting limits keep the price at a level every farm can live on.

Every farm family has a right to a fair chance at selling its crops. One farm growing far more than the rest takes that chance away. Planting limits, set by the county farm office, keep the market open to everyone. You can still farm as well as you like, up to the limit.

Nobody should get ahead by pushing their neighbors down. What the big farms grow beyond their fair share belongs to the valley, not to them. The council should ban the crop that's flooding the market and share out the extra, so every farm ends up on the same footing.

answer.moral_rights: You stood up for your rights. You said it's yours, and nobody else gets a say. The council heard both sides, and you won the point.
answer.practical: You said control wouldn't work. But you never said it was wrong. So nobody pushed back on the idea that control is the right thing to do.
answer.moral_common_good: You argued about what's best for everyone. That's the other side's favorite argument, and on that ground, they won.
answer.moral_positive_right: You ended up arguing for more control yourself.
answer.moral_collective: You ended up arguing for more control yourself.
